title: Ashtabula in Pendleton: Inside one of the Upstate's most haunted homes
excerpt: Ashtabula has been reported as one of the Upstate’s most haunted destinations.
content:
PENDLETON, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Ashtabula has been reported as one of the Upstate’s most haunted destinations.

Built in the 1820s by Lewis Gibbes as a family home, Ashtabula was never full. Gibbes’ wife died suddenly before construction was complete. Some say she has been seen standing outside the front door waiting to be let in, as one tourist photo purportedly shows.

Pam Patterson, with the Pendleton Historic Foundation, has led tours at Ashtabula for years. He said staff believe that spirits remain, tied as much to objects left behind as to the house itself.

“It’s not so much the house is haunted; it’s the possessions of the people who lived here, the things they left behind that make it haunted, the things that they’ve left their stamp on,” she said.

Each room has its own tale. In what staff call the most active room, set up as a young man’s room, Patterson said a door opened and then closed on its own while she was speaking to guests.

Others report whispers in the hallway, and video captured by a visitor appears to show a piano playing by itself.

Patterson said Ashtabula has a relatively dark history.

“We actually have some board members who don’t like to come here because they say something terrible happened here,” she said.

Some believe the grounds held bad energy before the home was built. The nearby tavern dates to about 1790, around the time Pendleton was established.

Patterson recounts a killing there involving a family: “The younger son was shot by the father, the older son killed the father and then ran.”

“Whether it was the darkness of Ashtabula or if it was just the way he was that made it happen, we don’t know,” she said.

The Pendleton Historic Foundation hosts tours year-round. Its ghost tours are currently sold out, but organizers have added one more showing on Nov. 7. Tickets can be purchased here.
